what: Boeing designs and builds commercial jets, defence aircraft and space systems, and services the aircraft already flying. With Airbus it forms the duopoly that supplies the world's large passenger jets.
customers: Airlines and leasing companies for jets; the US government and allied governments for defence and space.
money: military aircraft, satellites, weapons and the Starliner capsule
parts, maintenance and training for aircraft already delivered
moat: Only two companies can build large passenger jets. Airlines are tied to a fleet type by pilot training, spare parts and maintenance, which makes switching expensive.
risks: Years of quality and safety problems left regulators capping 737 production
Fixed-price defence contracts have produced repeated large charges
Debt of roughly $46 billion built up through the crisis years
Any new safety incident would restart regulatory scrutiny
opportunities: A backlog of thousands of ordered aircraft gives years of work if it can build them
Raising monthly 737 and 787 output converts that backlog into cash
The services business earns steady, higher-margin revenue from the installed fleet
watch: Monthly 737 and 787 delivery rates and whether free cash flow turns sustainably positive.
